analysis.one_liner: Bars states from requiring food safety warnings stricter than federal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 21 Senate cosponsors, was sent to the Senate health committee, which held one hearing in July 2006 but never voted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop states from setting food safety warning requirements that differ from federal rules. Any state warning or food safety rule would have to be 'identical' to federal law unless the state won an exemption from the Health and Human Services Secretary or proved an imminent health hazard. States could keep some rules — freshness dates, organic labels, dietary supplement rules — but the state-by-state warning labels that food companies face today would largely disappear.
analysis.who_benefits: Packaged food manufacturers and grocery retailers gain the most: instead of tracking dozens of state warning and safety rules, they would face a single federal standard. Supporters argued this cuts compliance costs and ends a patchwork of inconsistent rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits states from establishing or keeping any food warning requirement that is not identical to federal law, replacing a patchwork of state rules with one national standard.

States could still petition the Secretary of Health and Human Services for an exemption, and could act unilaterally against an imminent health hazard, giving industry a predictable, single set of rules instead of dozens of divergent ones.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers in states with stronger-than-federal food warning laws would lose those protections unless the state won a federal exemption. State governments would lose their ability to act faster or more strictly than Washington on food hazards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and states with stricter food rules

drawbacks.text: States would lose the power to require warnings about food hazards — including warnings about substances linked to cancer or reproductive harm — unless their rule matched federal law exactly or they obtained a federal exemption, leaving consumers with only whatever warnings the federal government chooses to require.

The exemption and petition process hands the decision to the federal Health and Human Services Secretary: a state that petitions to keep a stricter rule can be turned down, and if the Secretary formally rejects a proposal after public comment, the state may not enforce it at all.

Supporters' strongest argument in reply: a national standard avoids a confusing, expensive patchwork of 50 different labeling regimes, and the bill preserves states' rights to keep freshness dating, organic labeling, dietary supplement rules, and restaurant sanitation advisories.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Uniform national rules have real value — one label for one product is cheaper and simpler. But this bill achieves uniformity by pulling national standards down to the federal floor rather than up: any state that wanted to warn consumers sooner or more clearly than the FDA would have to win permission from Washington. The cost falls on consumers in the stricter states, while the savings go to food companies.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2006 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held one hearing in July 2006 but never voted to send the bill to the floor; it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Burr introduced the bill on May 25, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on July 27, 2006, printed as S.Hrg. 109-741, but took no further action.
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors — 20 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but never received a Senate floor vote and expired when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments kept their authority to require food safety warnings, and consumers in stricter states kept those protections; food manufacturers gained nothing and continue to face state-by-state rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and consumers kept local food warning powers

against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, arguing it would erase state food safety warnings such as those on chemicals linked to cancer or reproductive harm.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 20 of 55 Senate Republicans and a single Democrat — and the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no roll call to break down.

industries.note: The bill would erase state-specific food warning requirements — including state warnings on substances linked to cancer or reproductive harm — unless they matched federal law exactly, cutting the industry's compliance and labeling costs while leaving consumers with only federal-level warnings.
A single national warning standard would simplify stocking and labeling across states. The savings would come from standards being set at the federal level rather than by stricter states.
States would lose the power to require warnings or food safety rules stricter than federal law, keeping only a narrow petition process and an imminent-hazard exception.
